--- title: "Exercise 5: Bikeshare Wrangling" draft: true execute: echo: false --- In this exercise, we'll continue our study of the bike sharing data, but we’re starting to take off the training wheels: rather than using pre-wrangled data, you’ll be doing some of the data wrangling yourself! In this exercise you'll: - *refine* your skills in creating reproducible documents (Quarto) and graphics (Plotly) - *practice* grouping and aggregation functions in pandas - *see* some ways to work with dates ## Getting Started Create a folder for this exercise and create a new Quarto file in that folder named `ex05-bikeshare-wrangling.qmd`. Start with the usual setup code, given in the [course notes](../../notes/quarto.qmd#class-standards). ## Load Data We downloaded the data from the [Capital BikeShare program](https://www.capitalbikeshare.com/system-data). Note the license agreement there. We removed some columns of the data that we aren't using to reduce the size of the dataset you have to download. ::: {.callout collapse="true" title="Low-level wrangling code"} If you're really curious, here's the code I used to make the parquet files. For this exercise, though, just used the provided data files. ::: {#7240f7ee .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import requests, zipfile, io, pathlib import pandas as pd import numpy as np import glob for year in [2011, 2012]: parquet_filename = f'data/bikeshare_{year}.parquet' if pathlib.Path(parquet_filename).exists(): continue filenames = sorted(glob.glob(f"data/{year}*tripdata.csv")) if not filenames: print("Downloading", year, "data") url = f"https://s3.amazonaws.com/capitalbikeshare-data/{year}-capitalbikeshare-tripdata.zip" r = requests.get(url) z = zipfile.ZipFile(io.BytesIO(r.content)) z.extractall("data") filenames = sorted(glob.glob(f"data/{year}*tripdata.csv")) df = pd.concat([ pd.read_csv(filename, usecols=["Duration", "Start date", "Member type"], parse_dates=["Start date"]) for filename in filenames], ignore_index=True) df.rename(columns={"Start date": "start_time", "Duration": "duration", "Member type": "rider_type"}, inplace=True) df.to_parquet(parquet_filename, index=False) ``` ::: ::: We'll distribute the data for this exercise in a format called [Parquet](https://parquet.apache.org/), an efficient emerging standard for dataframe interchange. You can [read Parquet files with pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/io.html#parquet). The data files are broken up by year. Here we read in the data for 2011, which is the first of the two years included in the dataset for previous exercises. **Download the data file [here](https://calvin-data-science.github.io/data202/data/bikeshare/bikeshare_2011.parquet)** and upload it to a `data` folder in your exercise folder. ::: {#7a7af6a8 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} rides_2011 = pd.read_parquet("data/bikeshare_2011.parquet") rides = rides_2011 rides.info() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` RangeIndex: 1226767 entries, 0 to 1226766 Data columns (total 3 columns): # Column Non-Null Count Dtype --- ------ -------------- ----- 0 duration 1226767 non-null int64 1 start_time 1226767 non-null datetime64[ns] 2 rider_type 1226767 non-null object dtypes: datetime64[ns](1), int64(1), object(1) memory usage: 28.1+ MB ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="2012 data"} Once you've finished with this exercise, you can use the following instructions to load the 2012 data also. 1. Download the data file [here](https://calvin-data-science.github.io/data202/data/bikeshare/bikeshare_2012.parquet) 2. Upload it to the `data` folder. 3. Use the following code to load it and concatenate it with the 2011 data (replacing the `rides = rides_2011` line above): ```{{python}} rides_2012 = pd.read_parquet("data/bikeshare_2012.parquet") rides = pd.concat([rides_2011, rides_2012], ignore_index=True) ``` ::: Each row is a *ride*. For each ride we're given the start time of the trip, its duration, and rider type. ::: {.column-margin} According to the website: Member Type – Indicates whether user was a "registered" member (Annual Member, 30-Day Member or Day Key Member) or a "casual" rider (Single Trip, 24-Hour Pass, 3-Day Pass or 5-Day Pass) ::: ## Part 1: Inspecting the data ### Part 1A: Basic information Report some basic size and content information about the `rides` data frame. For example, how many rows and columns does it have? What are the data types of the columns? What fact does the first row of the data tell us? You may wish to refer to the data dictionary given on the [Capital BikeShare program](https://www.capitalbikeshare.com/system-data) website. Checklist: - [ ] You reported the number of rows and columns in the data frame (ideally using [a computation](../../notes/quarto.qmd#computations-in-text)). - [ ] You reported the data types (both storage and logical) of the columns. - [ ] You wrote a sentence conveying the information that the first row of the data tells us. ### Part 1B: `duration` column Note that the data dictionary does not specify the units of the `duration` column. It turns out that this is in seconds. **Confirm this by computing summary statistics of the `duration` column.** If you wish to make a plot, use `rides.sample(n=1000)` to get a random sample of 1000 rows, since the full dataset pushes the limits of what Plotly can plot efficiently. Use your domain knowledge about bike riding and cities to check whether the summary statistics make sense. For example, what is the longest ride you would expect to see? What is the shortest ride you would expect to see? What is the typical ride length? Finally, for practice, make a `duration_minutes` column that expresses the duration in minutes instead of seconds. Remember that there are 60 seconds in a minute. Checklist: - [ ] You computed summary statistics of the `duration` column. - [ ] You wrote a sentence or two explaining how one or two of those summary statistics make sense in the context of bike riding and cities. - [ ] You wrote code to create a `duration_minutes` column. ### Part 1C: `start_time` column What are the earliest and latest start times in the dataset? Look at the first and last rows in the dataframe, and check your observations using `min` and `max` methods on the column. Checklist: - [ ] You reported the first and last start times in the dataset. - [ ] You checked your observations using `min` and `max` methods on the column. ### Part 1D: `rider_type` column Make a table that shows how many rides were taken by registered riders and how many were taken by non-registered riders. Example result: ::: {#e90979b4 .cell execution_count=9} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ```{=html}
rider_type size
0 Casual 246949
1 Member 979814
2 Unknown 4
``` ::: ::: What does this table tell you that the data dictionary did not tell you? Checklist: - [ ] Your report includes a table showing the number of rides by rider type. - [ ] You wrote a short sentence containing the new piece of information that the table tells you. ## Part 2: Counting Rides By Day Our goal is to create a dataframe like the one used in [Exercise 1](../01intro/ex01-warmup.qmd) that includes the number of rides in each day. We'll do this in two steps: ### Part 2A: Date Wrangling The `start_time` column gives the timestamp (date and time) of when the ride started. We want to count the number of rides per day, so we need to extract the date from the timestamp. We can use the [`dt` accessor](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/basics.html#basics-dt-accessors) to access the date part of the timestamp: ::: {#acbd6516 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} rides['date'] = rides['start_time'].dt.date ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="other dt accessors"} The original dataframe also had columns for year, month, and day broken out. We won't need these (you can derive them all from `year`), but if you want them, you can use the [`dt` accessor](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/basics.html#basics-dt-accessors) (short for "datetime"). For example: ```python rides['year'] = rides['start_time'].dt.year ``` ::: Check that the first few rows look like: ::: {#12890be1 .cell execution_count=11} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ```{=html}
duration start_time rider_type date
0 3548 2011-01-01 00:01:29 Member 2011-01-01
1 346 2011-01-01 00:02:46 Casual 2011-01-01
2 562 2011-01-01 00:06:13 Member 2011-01-01
``` ::: ::: (All of the code for this part has been provided for you above; you just need to include it in your document.) ### Part 2B: Counting Count the number of rides for each date. Call the result `daily_rides`. The first few rows of result should look like: ::: {#40223df0 .cell execution_count=12} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ```{=html}
date total_rides
0 2011-01-01 959
1 2011-01-02 781
2 2011-01-03 1301
3 2011-01-04 1536
4 2011-01-05 1571
``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip} To get the column to be named `total_rides` instead of `size`, you can either use an explicit aggregation, or rename the result using `.rename(columns={'size': 'total_rides'})`. Remember that by default, `DataFrame` methods return a *new* `DataFrame`, so you can just include the `rename` in the method chain. ::: ::: {.callout-note title="Data Types"} The resulting `date` column is a `datetime.date` object, which is a Python object that represents a date (but not a time). pandas and Plotly don't handle this type of object well, so let's convert it to a `datetime` object. You can convert a column to a `datetime` object using `pd.to_datetime`: ::: {#e1124ff5 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} daily_rides['date'] = pd.to_datetime(daily_rides['date']) ``` ::: ::: Checklist: - [ ] You created a `daily_rides` data frame that contains the number of rides per day. - [ ] You converted the `date` column to a `datetime` object using the provided code. ### Part 2C: Validating the result How many rows does `daily_rides` have? How many rows *should* it have, given your knowledge of how calendars work? If the number of rows is different, what might be the cause? Checklist: - [ ] You reported the number of rows in the `daily_rides` data frame. - [ ] You reported the number of rows that you expected. - [ ] You wrote a sentence about what you (didn't) observe. ### Part 2D: Recreating a plot from Exercise 1 Recreate the "total number of rides by day" plot we made in Exercise 1: ::: {#9fa6bfd8 .cell execution_count=14} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} When I first tried adding a trendline like we did, I hit a Plotly / pandas bug about `date` (not `datetime`) columns. If you also get a `TypeError`, see above for code for how to use `pd.to_datetime` to convert the column to a `datetime` column. ::: Checklist: - [ ] You made a plot of total rides by date (anything beyond that is nice to have, but not required) ## Part 3: Breaking down by rider type Repeat Part 2, but now create a `daily_rides_by_type` data frame where you break down the counts by rider type, like we did in [Exercise 2](../01intro/ex02-bikeshare.qmd). For example: ::: {#ad767b97 .cell execution_count=15} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ```{=html}
date rider_type rides
0 2011-01-01 Casual 330
1 2011-01-01 Member 629
2 2011-01-02 Casual 130
3 2011-01-02 Member 651
4 2011-01-03 Casual 120
``` ::: ::: Hint: you can group by multiple columns by passing a list of column names to `groupby`. **Make sure you validate the shape of this data frame also**; there *is* a difference between the number of rows you expect and the number of rows you get. Fix the issue by using a `query` to remove a small number of rows. Use the `daily_rides_by_type` data frame to recreate the plot from Exercise 2: ::: {#365a60c4 .cell execution_count=18} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Part 4: Breaking down by day of week Recreate the "How does ridership vary over a typical week?" plot using this dataset. ::: {.callout-note title="Day of Week column"} You'll need to add a column for the day of the week. Use the [`strftime` method](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.dt.strftime.html) to get the name of the day of the week. We also need to convert the resulting column to a `Categorical` column so that Plotly will plot the days in the correct order and pandas will order the rows correctly when we group by day of week. Here's how I did it (admittedly with some help from GitHub Copilot!): ::: {#5b6b1044 .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Extract day of week daily_rides_by_type['day_of_week'] = daily_rides_by_type['date'].dt.strftime("%a") # Convert to an ordered Categorical daily_rides_by_type['day_of_week'] = pd.Categorical( daily_rides_by_type['day_of_week'], categories=["Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun"], ordered=True ) ``` ::: We're not going to study Categorical columns very much, but they're useful when dealing with qualitative data, especially when it's ordered. You can read more about them [here](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/categorical.html). ::: ::: {.callout-note title="Other notes"} - Omit the "Unknown" rider type (if you haven't already) - If you're only using the 2011 rides, the specific values will be a bit different than what you saw in Exercise 2 because that also included 2012. You can add the 2012 data too if you like; see the notes at the beginning of the exercise. ::: For reference, here's what I got when I used this dataset: ::: {#577eaef2 .cell execution_count=20} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: Show the same summary as the plot above, but in tabular form. ::: {#e12e9d9f .cell execution_count=21} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=21} ```{=html}
day_of_week rider_type median_rides

1 Mon Member 3236.5
